'''Felisa A. Smith''' is an American ecologist who is a Distinguished Professor at the [[University of New Mexico]]. She is a conservation [[paleoecology|paleoecologist]] who uses fossil records to understand the pressing environmental issues such as the climate crisis and biodiversity loss. She has served as President of the [[American Society of Mammalogists]] and the [[International Biogeography Society]]. She was awarded the 2022 [[C. Hart Merriam Award]] by the American Society of Mammalogists and is a Fellow of the Paleontology Society.

== Early life and education ==
Smith's mother, [[Maria del Carmen Calvo Herrero]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Nelson |first=Toni |date=2019-07-24 |title=In Memoriam, Renowned Artist, Maria del Carmen Calvo |url=https://patch.com/california/lagunaniguel-danapoint/memoriam-renowned-artist-maria-del-carmen-calvo |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=Laguna Niguel-Dana Point, CA Patch |language=en}}</ref> was an artist, and her father, Frank Smith, was a civil engineer. She studied biology, literature and visual arts at the [[University of California, San Diego]]. After graduating, Smith worked as a high school science teacher at [[Laguna Hills High School]]. Smith focused on ecology and evolutionary biology at the [[University of California, Irvine]] for her graduate studies.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Felisa A. Smith :: Department of Biology {{!}} The University of New Mexico |url=https://biology.unm.edu/people/faculty/profile/smith_felisa-a.html |access-date=2026-02-09 |website=biology.unm.edu}}</ref> For her doctoral research, Smith investigated [[neotoma]] (pack rat) populations.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nutritional ecology and body size in Neotoma populations {{!}} WorldCat.org |url=https://search.worldcat.org/title/27058580 |access-date=2026-02-09 |website=search.worldcat.org |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Wright |first=Karen |date=1993-09-01 |title=Revelations of Rat Scat |url=https://www.discovermagazine.com/revelations-of-rat-scat-39969 |access-date=2026-02-11 |website=Discover Magazine |language=en}}</ref> She used fossils to understand whether pack rats obeyed [[Bergmann's rule]], that the body size of a mammal is inversely proportional to the temperature of their environment.<ref name=":2" />

== Research and career ==
Smith was a NSF Postdoctoral Fellow with [[James Brown (ecologist)|James H. Brown]]. After some time as a research professor, Smith joined the tenure-track faculty at the [[University of New Mexico]] in 2006.{{citation needed|date=February 2026}} She combines historic and fossil records with modern biology to understand the impact of climate change on biodiversity and the effects of loss of biodiversity on ecosystems. Her early work considered the abilities of small mammals to adapt to climate change. The [[paleomidden]] record provided Smith an opportunity to explore the relationship between rodent body size and temperature over 25,000 years. She showed that body size was linked to the size of fecal pellets, and used fossil fecal pellets to understand body size.{{citation needed|date=February 2026}}

Smith has studied organisms across multiple sizes, from microbes to mammoths.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Appointments Chart :: Office for Academic Personnel {{!}} The University of New Mexico |url=https://oap.unm.edu/faculty/featured-faculty/felisa-smith.html |access-date=2026-02-10 |website=oap.unm.edu}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=What will happen if modern large mammals become extinct? |url=https://www.earth.com/news/what-will-happen-if-modern-large-mammals-become-extinct/ |access-date=2026-02-10 |website=Earth.com |language=en}}</ref> For example, she has studied the fossil record during the [[megafauna extinction]], and found that ratios of carbon and nitrogen stable isotopes in plants (δ<sup>13</sup>C and δ<sup>15</sup>N) had shifted, indicative of changing animal diets.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title="The Missing Pieces: Lost Ecological Function following the Terminal Pleistocene Megafaunal Extinction" {{!}} University of Kentucky College of Arts & Sciences |url=https://www.as.uky.edu/smith-seminar |access-date=2026-02-10 |website=www.as.uky.edu}}</ref>

Between the [[pleistocene]] and [[holocene]], Smith found that some animals grew larger and some got smaller. Moreover, the loss of megafauna led to shifts in the ecology and size of [https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2115015119#abstract surviving mammals]. She has argued that the ongoing biodiversity loss due to human activities and [[climate change]] could have the same impact [[megafauna]].<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Research team looks to past for insights on future of megafauna |url=https://news.unm.edu/news/research-team-looks-to-past-for-insights-on-future-of-megafauna |access-date=2026-02-10 |website=UNM UCAM Newsroom |language=en}}</ref> She has demonstrated that the offspring of [[carnivorous dinosaur]]s reduced species diversity by taking on the role of multiple species as they grew.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Did teenage 'tyrants' outcompete other dinosaurs? |url=https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/490218 |access-date=2026-02-10 |website=EurekAlert! |language=en}}</ref> Smith also showed that the loss of large mammals impacted biogeochemical cycles around the world, and contributed to the drop in methane which is associated with the [[Younger Dryas]], a colder interval in the late [[Pleistocene]].{{citation needed|date=February 2026}}

==Awards and honors==
In 2020, Smith was elected Fellow of the [[Paleontological Society]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=UNM professor selected as a Fellow of the Paleontological Society |url=https://news.unm.edu/news/unm-professor-selected-as-a-fellow-of-paleontological-society |access-date=2026-02-10 |website=UNM UCAM Newsroom |language=en}}</ref> The following year, she was elected President of the American Society of Mammalogists and the [[International Biogeography Society]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=F |first=Karen |title=Past Board Members |url=https://www.biogeography.org/about-us/board/past-board-members/ |access-date=2026-02-10 |website=The International Biogeography Society |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2018-12-28 |title=Felisa Smith to the Lead the International Biogeography Society |url=https://wiareport.com/2018/12/felisa-smith-to-the-lead-the-international-biogeography-society/ |access-date=2026-02-10 |website=Women In Academia Report |language=en-US}}</ref> She was the first hispanic woman to hold such a position.<ref>{{Cite web |title=UNM professor elected president elect of American Society of Mammalogists |url=https://news.unm.edu/news/unm-professor-elected-president-elect-of |access-date=2026-02-10 |website=UNM UCAM Newsroom |language=en}}</ref> In 2022, she was awarded the American Society of Mammalogists Merriam Award.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Smith receives prestigious Merriam award |url=https://news.unm.edu/news/smith-receives-prestigious-merriam-award |access-date=2026-02-10 |website=UNM UCAM Newsroom |language=en}}</ref> In 2023, she was honored with the [[University of New Mexico Ovation Award]], named the 68th Annual Research Lecturer and a Distinguished |url=https://news.unm.edu/news/unm-announces-68th-annual-research-lectureship-for-career-achievement-honoree |access-date=2026-02-10 |website=UNM UCAM Newsroom |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web == Personal life ==
{{BLP unreferenced section|date=February 2026}}
Smith has two daughters, Emma, a historical geochemist, and Rosemary, a theoretical mathematician. She is married to Scott M. Elliott, a chemist at [[Los Alamos National Laboratory]].
